core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Interstitial Cystitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome is a diagnosis of exclusion; begin with education, bladder and dietary strategies, pelvic-floor physical therapy when indicated, and individualized multimodal treatment after excluding infection, hematuria causes, and gynecologic disease.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: chronic pelvic pain relieved by urinating, frequency
Key HPI features: a 62-year-old woman has chronic pelvic pain relieved by voiding and urinary frequency.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Interstitial Cystitis.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Interstitial Cystitis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Urinary tract infection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Labeling symptoms as bladder pain syndrome without evaluating infection, hematuria, pelvic malignancy, or other gynecologic and gastrointestinal causes.
management_principles: Start with education, symptom and voiding diaries, dietary/bladder strategies, and pelvic-floor therapy when appropriate; consider medications only through shared decision-making after reviewing adverse effects and contraindications.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of chronic pelvic pain relieved by urinating, frequency. HPI: interstitial cystitis.
reference_soap.objective: Obtain urinalysis and culture; assess for hematuria and perform focused abdominal and pelvic evaluation as indicated. Consider further evaluation for atypical symptoms or malignancy risk.
reference_soap.assessment: Possible interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome after exclusion of infection and other urinary, gynecologic, and gastrointestinal causes.
reference_soap.plan: Begin education, bladder/dietary trigger review, and a symptom diary; consider pelvic-floor physical therapy and individualized non-opioid symptom management. Refer for persistent, atypical, or red-flag symptoms; do not use antibiotics without evidence of infection.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Interstitial Cystitis
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Interstitial Cystitis
Use an exclusion-based, multimodal management approach for bladder pain syndrome

teaching.one_liner: Urology evaluation for patient presenting with chronic pelvic pain relieved by urinating, frequency.
differentials: Endometriosis or chronic pelvic pain syndrome
red_flags: Gross hematuria, unexplained weight loss, or a pelvic mass
Fever, flank pain, or systemic illness suggesting infection or obstruction

must_ask.objective: Pain relationship to bladder filling and voiding
must_ask.say: Does the pain get worse as your bladder fills, and does it improve right after you urinate?
How many times a day do you need to urinate, and how is that affecting your life?
Have your urine cultures come back negative for infection?
Have you noticed foods or drinks like coffee, alcohol, or spicy food that make the pain worse?
How long have you had this pelvic pain and frequency — has it been more than six months?
